title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
hookLine: scrolls hidden in caves at Qumran, found in modern times

cards: A stone goes into a dark hole in a cliff, and something inside breaks.
That's the story usually told: a shepherd in the hills above the Dead Sea, looking for a stray animal, tosses a rock into a cave and hears pottery crack.
Inside are clay jars, and inside the jars, rolled-up scrolls, written in Hebrew and Aramaic. More caves follow, near a place called Qumran, some holding scrolls, some only scraps.
They had been sitting in the dark, in a dry desert, the whole time, waiting.

teach.h: PUT THEM IN AN EARTHEN VESSEL.
teach.b: Keeping writing in clay jars isn't a new idea; the Tanakh itself describes it. In the book of Jeremiah, with Babylon at the gates, the prophet buys a field, and the deed is to be put away.
In the King James words: "put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days." A clay jar, so the words last. In the caves near Qumran, scrolls turned up in clay jars too.
Among them are copies of books of the Bible, written out by hand.

teach.h: A COMMUNITY'S OWN RULES AND HYMNS.
teach.b: Beside them are writings of a community's own: rules for a community that lived together and shared what it had, hymns, and commentaries reading the prophets as if they spoke about the readers' own day.

Some scholars connect that community with the Essenes Josephus described; others see it differently. Nobody knows for certain who hid the scrolls, or exactly why. Maybe for safekeeping in a dangerous time.
Jewish tradition has its own word for that: genizah, a place where worn-out holy writings are put away instead of thrown out.
The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, tells of Rabban Gamliel the Elder being brought a translation of the book of Job. He had the builder set it under a course of stones: out of use, but not thrown away.

how: A synagogue may keep a genizah for worn-out books and pages that contain God's name, burying or storing them rather than throwing them away, and visitors to the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem can see some of the scrolls on display.

games.q: you have a worn-out holy scroll, too damaged to read from. it has God's name in it. what does Jewish tradition do?
o: throw it away with the trash.
put it away in a genizah, hidden, not thrown out.
keep reading from it as it is.
games.why: worn holy writings go into a genizah, stored or buried. the Talmud tells of Rabban Gamliel ordering a book hidden away under stones.

practice: If you can, find a photo of a Dead Sea scroll and just look, not at the captions, but at the lines of letters, the cracks, the dark edges.
If you can't, picture a clay jar with a rolled scroll inside and the cave going quiet around it.
Stay with the hands that wrote it and carried it into the dark, and if you pray, give thanks in words from your tradition for those who kept the words safe.

wordCard.voice: Genizah. A place where worn-out holy writings are put away instead of thrown out, the word Jewish tradition uses for scrolls hidden away like those found near Qumran. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a scroll, as in megillah, a rolled book of writing.
